meta.title: Conflict Watchlist
meta.notes: Fully automated register: a scheduled open-source review rewrites this file daily (procedure in docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md) and an hourly GitHub Action refreshes the live reporting feed (watchlist-live.json) from GDELT. Every comparison the dashboard shows (state moves, changed dimensions, the attention-score bonuses) is made against the register as it stood compareDays (7) days ago, taken from each item's `snapshots` (one entry per review: date, state and the five dimensions). Each review: (1) set reviewDate/previousReviewDate, (2) for every item set the new `now` on the five dimensions and the new `state`, then append today's snapshot (keep the last 60), (3) rewrite `status` (`summary`: plain-language current status whose first sentence states the newest development; `sources`: 2–3 links to the newest reporting), `whyNow`, `topic` and `whyMatters` (stable framing, revise only on a phase change), `changes` (dated bullets covering the last 7 days: keep those still inside the window, add today's, drop older ones), `next`, `ignore` and `sources`, (4) record any state move in `history` and keep `timeline` (4–8 dated one-line events of the current phase, chronological) current. The dashboard derives attention rank, movements, changed-dimension flags, staleness, coverage surges — do not type those in. `next` holds named, checkable indicators.

Priority.desc: Direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value.

Active.desc: Material trend, escalation, or regional relevance.

phase.label: Conflict phase
phase.desc: A short label for the stage the conflict is in (for example attritional war, ceasefire without implementation, grey-zone contest). It sits under the current-status summary and shows the label from 7 days ago when it changed.

escalation.label: Escalation risk
escalation.desc: How likely a step up in intensity or a change of phase is in the coming weeks.

levels.Low: Stable; no live trigger and restraints hold.
levels.Moderate: Triggers exist (deadlines, disputes, incidents) but restraints are holding.
levels.High: Active exchanges or a named trigger that is likely to fire; a phase change is plausible within weeks.
levels.Severe: Active war or ongoing kinetic exchange with strategic stakes (major shipping lanes, energy, great-power forces).

tempo.label: Operational tempo
tempo.desc: How much military activity is actually happening in the review window.

levels.Medium: Recurring incidents or steady, limited operations (patrols, fortification, occasional strikes).
levels.High: Daily strikes or operations across fronts.

adaptation.label: Adaptation behaviour
adaptation.desc: How much new tactical or technical behaviour appeared in the window; this is where the Army learning sits.

levels.Low: Both sides are using the same methods as before.
levels.High: Novel, repeatable adaptations appeared (new weapons employment, counter-measures, doctrine shifts).

sgExposure.label: Singapore exposure
sgExposure.desc: How directly the conflict touches Singapore's interests. Not shown as a register column; it still feeds the attention score and the expanded row.

levels.Moderate: An ASEAN or diplomatic role, observer contributions, or supply-chain spillover.
levels.High: Direct effect on sea lanes, energy or shipping, a Singapore-flagged vessel affected, or relevance to deployments.

attentionScore.desc: Deterministic, explainable rank. state (Priority 40 / Active 25 / Watch 10 / Archive 0) + escalation risk (Severe 20 / High 15 / Moderate 8 / Low 2) + 5 per dimension that changed over the last 7 days (compareDays) + 10 if the state moved up over the same window + Singapore exposure (High 8 / Moderate 4 / Low 0) + tier (T1 6 / T2 3 / T3 0) + 8 if the live open-source feed shows a coverage surge (see definitions.feed.surgeRule). Items flagged ignore-for-now are shown but ranked last.

feed.source: GDELT DOC 2.0 API (open, no key). Per item: 30-day daily article counts (TimelineVolRaw) and the most relevant English-language articles of the last 7 days (ArtList, HybridRel). Synced by .github/workflows/sync-watchlist-feed.yml into watchlist-live.json.
feed.surgeRule: A coverage surge is flagged when the last 7 days carry at least twice the article volume of the 7 days before and at least 20 articles; a surge adds 8 points to the attention score.
feed.titleFilter: Articles are kept only when the title contains one of the item's terms, to cut GDELT's full-text noise.
feed.terms: Title filter: at least one of these substrings must appear in an article title for it to count as reporting on the item.
feed.require: Optional groups of substrings; a title must contain at least one term from every group (two-party theatres: one term per side).
feed.exclude: Optional substrings that drop a title (sport, entertainment and other noise), in addition to the sync's global list.
feed.spamDomainsNote: Article sources dropped outright (livestream/score spam). The daily review adds domains seen producing noise.

columns.tier: Standing relevance to the Army: T1 Priority Conflicts, T2 Active Regional & Escalation Watches, T3 Baseline Regional Research Reserve. Tiers do not change week to week.
columns.state: Today's monitoring state: Priority (direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value), Active (material trend, escalation or regional relevance), Watch (baseline monitoring), Archive (reserve; revisit on a named trigger). ▲▼ marks a move over the last 7 days.
columns.status: Current status: the newest title-matched headline from the live open-source feed (synced hourly) on top, then a plain-language summary of what is happening now whose first sentence states the newest development, with links to the newest reporting it rests on. The phase label sits beneath; a struck-through label is the phase 7 days ago.
columns.coverage: Open-source coverage from the live feed (GDELT with Google News fallback): the sparkline is the last 30 days (or four weekly counts), the number is articles in the last 7 days with the change against the 7 before. 'Surge' = at least twice the prior week and at least 20 articles. Refreshes hourly.
columns.nextIndicator: The soonest dated indicator to watch, tagged with the numbered topic and watch area it informs (or 'cross-cutting' when it bears on the theatre as a whole). Expand the row for the full list.
columns.confidence: How well-sourced the assessment is: High (multiple independent, dated sources), Medium (some single-source or snippet-only items), Low (thin or contested reporting).
columns.attention: Attention score, the register's sort order. Hover a score for its breakdown.
columns.topic: Topics of interest: the three capability contests the Army follows this theatre for, set by the team (from the watchlist workbook). Numbered so they line up with the 'Why it matters' and 'Watch areas' columns; the chip is the topic's adaptability rating.
columns.whyMatters: Why it matters here: for each numbered topic, what the theatre tests (the capability, behaviour or mechanism under study).
columns.watchAreas: Watch areas: for each numbered topic, its watch status and what to monitor. Status tags: Rising (activity increasing), Established (steady pattern), Contested (the outcome is still open), Watch for trigger (review only on a named event), Background monitor, Declining.
columns.adaptability: Adaptability: how transferable the topic's lessons are to the Army — High, Medium or Low, set by the team.

watches.desc: Watches follow one thread of an item on its own once a trigger event makes it worth it: an information-operations watch (kind "info-ops": official messaging, state-media narratives and documented influence campaigns), a shadow-war watch (kind "shadow-war": sabotage, incursions, cyber and influence below the threshold of war, and the targeted side's responses) or an operation watch (kind "operation": one named military operation, its gains, the enemy's response and what it shows). Each carries a narrower daily feed, plus dated findings and an assessment researched from open sources at each review.

types.official statement: Government, foreign-ministry, military or party statement aimed at an audience (strategic communications).
types.state-media narrative: Framing pushed by state or party media, including English-language outlets aimed abroad.
types.covert information operation: Documented coordinated inauthentic behaviour, disinformation or cognitive-warfare activity, attributed by a credible reporter.
types.coercive signalling: Military, coast-guard or legal action whose purpose is the message it sends.
types.sanctions/lawfare: Sanctions, lists or legal framing used to pressure or delegitimise.
types.counter-messaging: The targeted side's official response or rebuttal.
types.domestic narrative: Narratives inside the targeted polity (parties, polls, viral claims).
types.debunked claim: A specific false claim identified by a fact-checker.
types.third-party assessment: Analysis by a think-tank, researcher or major outlet.
types.hybrid attack: Physical sabotage, arson, cable or pipeline damage, cyber attacks, GPS jamming, drone or airspace incursions and other deniable attacks below the threshold of war.
types.defensive response: The targeted side's practical countermeasures: arrests, expulsions, airspace closures, deployments, new laws and alliance consultations.
types.territorial change: Ground or settlements gained or lost, with who reports it and whether it is independently confirmed (geolocated footage, ISW).
types.official claim: A command's or ministry's claim of gains, enemy losses or prisoners that has not been independently confirmed.
types.counterattack: The opposing side's counterattacks, reinforcements or renewed assaults in the operation's sector.
types.tactic or capability: A tactic, weapon or enabler used in the operation (drones, electronic warfare, converted vehicles, shaping strikes).

items.whyNow: The first trilateral talks since February ended on 11 Nov with a prisoner-exchange deal but no ceasefire, and Russia struck Kyiv within hours while US envoys flew to Moscow, so the strike war, not diplomacy, is setting the winter terms. Russia's energy campaign left 13 oblasts on rolling blackouts by 9 Nov as Germany said its Patriot interceptor stocks for Ukraine were exhausted and Starshield speed limits returned to hamper interceptor drones.
changes: 12 Nov: Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow, where Putin claimed control of Kostiantynivka and proposed a humanitarian pause there, which Kyiv rejected; hours after the talks Russia hit Kyiv with ballistic and Zircon missiles and 123 drones, killing one; Zelensky said Starshield speed caps of about 161 km/h had returned, hampering interceptor drones against jet-powered Shaheds (Kyiv Independent).

11 Nov: The two-day Abu Dhabi talks ended with agreement on a large-scale prisoner exchange (1,000 or more each discussed, due in two to three weeks) but no ceasefire; Medinsky ruled out territorial exchanges and Lavrov restated Russia's June 2024 demands; two Russian Banderol missiles crossed Moldovan airspace (Al Jazeera, Meduza, ISW, Kyiv Independent).

10 Nov: Overnight into 11 Nov, Ukrainian drones hit the Ust-Luga oil terminals about 850 km from the border, closing 26 Russian airports temporarily, and later the Omsk refinery about 2,450 km away, while Russia's 163 drones struck six large substations in four oblasts (ISW).

9 Nov: Ukraine's energy ministry said Russia had hit energy, oil and gas sites 128 times since 2 Nov and that 13 oblasts had outages; Ukraine struck the Kirishi refinery and a solid-fuel plant supplying Iskander production; Russian attacks fell to 140 a day, the fewest since at least August (ISW).

8 Nov: About 600,000 people lost power in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast after a second night of strikes; Ukraine hit a bridge on the M-14 Rostov–Crimea highway; ISW reported October as Russia's highest-casualty month of the war and noted Russian infiltration around Dobropillya (ISW).

7 Nov: Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones, all the missiles at Kyiv and its region, hitting the Northern Bridge four times and a substation linking the Rivne and Khmelnytskyi nuclear plants; Germany said its Patriot interceptor stocks for Ukraine were exhausted; the Komyshuvakha toll rose to 55 (ISW, Kyiv Independent).

next.text: Whether the large-scale prisoner exchange agreed in Abu Dhabi on 11 Nov (1,000 or more each discussed; Russia's Zorin said within two to three weeks) is carried out in full.
next.ifSeen: Exchange of 1,000+ each completed → note for the monthly pattern set; delayed or shrunk → track only.

next.text: A further negotiating round after the Witkoff–Kushner meeting with Putin on 12 Nov, including any multilateral format with Europeans (which the Kremlin says it has no vision for), a Putin–Trump discussion at APEC, or acceptance of Putin's proposed humanitarian pause in Kostiantynivka.

next.text: Another Russian mass strike causing city-wide loss of water in Kyiv for more than 24 hours or more than 1 million households without power (13 oblasts on outages and 128 energy strikes in 2–9 Nov per the energy ministry), versus restoration within a day.
next.ifSeen: Repeat city-wide outage → escalate; restoration within 24 hours sustained → note for the monthly pattern set.

next.text: Patriot interceptor supply after Germany said on 7 Nov its stocks for Ukraine were exhausted, against salvos of 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv (7 Nov) and Russia's repeated bridge strikes.
next.ifSeen: Another Dnipro bridge in Kyiv closed or a further 30+ ballistic salvo largely unintercepted → escalate; new interceptor transfers confirmed → note for the monthly pattern set.

next.ifSeen: Fuel limits reimposed or Baltic exports curtailed → flag today; strikes halted under US pressure → track only.

timeline.text: Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps revealed Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive near Lyman it said cleared 75 square kilometres of Russian infiltrators and liberated Serednie and nearby villages.

Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones at energy sites around Kyiv and Kharkiv, leaving 600,000 without power, as the 3rd Army Corps claimed a fourth Vivaldi stage of 101 square kilometres north of Lyman.

Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia, setting fires at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and Ruchi depot and hitting a VK data centre about 850 km from the border, its deepest mass raid of the war.

A limited humanitarian ceasefire around occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast took effect for aid deliveries and evacuations, the first agreed local truce of the year, while Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles and 280 drones.
Russian glide bombs, including a FAB-3000, struck a school used as a humanitarian aid point in Komyshuvakha, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, and then a nearby shelter, killing at least 40 people.
Russia's largest strike on Ukraine's energy system this year hit power plants and substations in nine regions and caused emergency power cuts and widespread water outages in Kyiv.

Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones, all the missiles aimed at Kyiv and its region, hitting the city's Northern Bridge four times and a substation linking two nuclear plants to central Ukraine.
US-mediated trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi ended after two days with agreement on a large-scale prisoner exchange but no ceasefire and no movement on territory.

text: On persistent ISR versus signature management and deception, the Established and Contested status holds. ISW reported on 8 Nov that Russian units are fielding decoy mannequins and vehicles to fool Ukrainian drones with automated target recognition, and on 9 Nov that Russian attacks fell to 140, the lowest daily count since August, with no advances by either side; Putin's 12 Nov claim to hold Kostiantynivka, denied by Kyiv, shows observation-saturated ground still resists consolidation. On EW versus alternative UAS control and layered counter-UAS, the Rising status is borne out: Russia is adding turbojets and mesh modems to strike drones (ISW, 7 Nov), Ukraine struck a Russian Starlink-jamming station on 9 Nov, and an expert argued on 9 Nov that Iskander seekers defeat navigation jamming (single source), while returning Starshield speed caps on 12 Nov weakened Ukraine's interceptor-drone layer.

On contested sustainment versus dispersed support and repair, the Established and Contested status hardens. Russia's 128 energy strikes in 2–9 Nov and bridge hits in Kyiv on 7 Nov target throughput rather than front positions, while Ukraine's strikes from Ust-Luga to Omsk on 10–11 Nov and Russia's shift to drone logistics in the 30 km kill zone (8 Nov) show both sides now treating rear-area resilience as decisive.

findings.actor: Unidentified drones from Belarus; Lithuanian crisis centre and NATO air policing
findings.tactic: Drone incursions from Belarus closing airports
findings.text: On the night of 10-11 Nov 2026 suspected drones from Belarus triggered two air alerts, one rising to red with residents told to shelter, and Vilnius and Kaunas airports were temporarily closed, disrupting three flights and more than 400 passengers; Latvia activated drone interceptors as one drone crossed into its airspace. NATO jets were scrambled twice and detected an object but did not shoot it down, so the disruption worked and interception again did not; no operator has been identified (single source).

findings.actor: Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) National Cyberint Center
findings.tactic: Stopping FSB-linked Turla email intrusion
findings.text: SRI disclosed on 11 Nov 2026 that Turla, a group linked to Russia's FSB, had breached an unnamed Romanian government body in December 2025 by exploiting Microsoft vulnerabilities, using malware ESET says hunts for NATO and EU emails. SRI says its Cyberint centre stopped the attack with EU and NATO partners, no exfiltration of sensitive data was found and the email service was fixed; the result rests on SRI's own account.

findings.actor: Polish Internal Security Agency (ABW)
findings.tactic: Arresting paid arson and reconnaissance cell
findings.text: Poland's ABW arrested two Ukrainians aged 24 and 25, announced on 10 Nov 2026, suspected of photographing critical infrastructure and military sites, setting cars on fire and swapping in Ukrainian military number plates, for pay partly in cryptocurrency on behalf of Russian intelligence. The car arsons had already happened, but the cell is now in three-month custody facing 10 years to life, the latest in a run of Polish and German roll-ups of disposable proxy agents.

findings.actor: UK Counter Terrorism Policing with the FBI and US military
findings.tactic: Arrest of NATO-corps officer for espionage
findings.text: On 10 Nov 2026 British counter-terrorism police arrested a 41-year-old US Army officer serving with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service, which US and UK officials linked to Russia, under the National Security Act. Searches continue and no allegation has been detailed, so whether a penetration of an allied headquarters was cut off or already did damage is unknown.

findings.actor: Unidentified senders (signed 'Male State' and 'Mikhail Andropov'; no state attribution)
findings.tactic: Mass hoax bomb threats against flights
findings.text: From 2 to 6 Nov 2026 emailed bomb threats hit flights and airports across Europe, disrupting at least 30 flights on 5 Nov with diversions and fighter escorts, and on 6 Nov reached RTE, Nova TV and Sky News, forcing RTE to evacuate its Dublin headquarters; the emails demanded an end to aid for Ukraine. All were hoaxes, but the low-cost tactic achieved repeated disruption; Spain called it hybrid aggression while no state has been named and Male State's founder denied involvement.

findings.actor: European air forces, NATO aircraft and police
findings.tactic: Fighter escorts and diversions against hoaxes
findings.text: Authorities answered the 2-6 Nov 2026 threat wave with coordinated national procedures, NATO fighter escorts, searches and diversions; no device was found, nobody was hurt and Eurocontrol called overall disruption minimal. Deterrence failed so far: threats continued daily, the only detention, at Schiphol on 5 Nov, ended in release, and no sender has been identified, with security experts due to meet in Brussels the following week.

findings.actor: Polish police, Border Guard, army and intelligence services
findings.tactic: Pre-emptive security operation on Kaliningrad border
findings.text: On 2 Nov 2026 Polish police launched a special operation with counter-terrorism units along the Kaliningrad border in Warmia-Masuria and Podlasie after military and allied intelligence warned of possible sabotage, possibly including armed groups crossing the border. On the night of 2-3 Nov border guards saw people with flashlights near Sępopol and authorities said they had prevented a Russian provocation, but no crossing was confirmed and Tusk said the intent could not be established, so whether the deployment deterred an attack is unproven.

findings.actor: NATO (Baltic Sentry naval and air presence)
findings.tactic: Persistent patrols over Baltic undersea infrastructure
findings.text: NATO Assistant Secretary General Christian Buck told the European Parliament defence committee on 3 Nov 2026 that only one undersea-infrastructure incident, limited in scope, has occurred in the Baltic since Baltic Sentry began in January 2025, the last in January 2026, and that Russia has shifted to other domains. On that account the anchor-dragging pattern of 2023-2025 has been suppressed, but the figures are NATO's own and Buck conceded NATO cannot block shadow-fleet ships in peacetime or operate in the Black Sea (single source).

findings.actor: Unidentified hackers (no attribution; Russia suspected by some officials)
findings.tactic: Remote takeover of supermarket refrigeration controllers
findings.text: Overnight into 2 Nov 2026 fridges and freezers ran hot at more than 100 shops in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia, with temperatures in some cases set to 50°C, after a similar mid-October attack on hundreds of French stores. Attackers used internet-exposed, often end-of-life controllers with weak passwords; Belgian prosecutors opened an investigation and the EU agriculture commissioner called it a deliberate attempt to disrupt food supply. No one has claimed it and no government has attributed it to Russia, so its place in the Russian campaign is unproven.

findings.actor: Romanian Air Force (MApN)
findings.tactic: Scrambling F-16s against drone incursion
findings.text: On the evening of 31 Oct 2026 two drones entered north-eastern Romania during Russian strikes on Ukraine; Romania scrambled four F-16s and an IAR-330 helicopter and warned residents of six counties. One drone left Romanian airspace and the other was last tracked on the Vaslui-Bacău border; neither was reported shot down, so detection and warning worked but interception again did not.

findings.actor: Swedish police (border police, Stockholm region)
findings.tactic: Boarding suspected drone-depot cargo ship
findings.text: Overnight into 31 Oct 2026 Swedish police boarded an 80-metre dry-cargo ship with a Russian crew off north-west Gotland; TV4 reported that its owner is investigated over suspected use of its ships as depots for Russian intelligence drones near drone alarms across Europe. Police described a routine border check and said the documents raised no remarks, so the boarding produced no detention or public evidence (single source for the drone-depot suspicion).

assessment.text: Between 30 Oct and 12 Nov the Russia-suspected campaign leaned on cheap, deniable tools that cost defenders far more than attackers. Hoax bomb threats from 2 to 6 Nov forced diversions or fighter escorts for more than 30 flights and emptied RTE's headquarters; no device was found and no state has been named, and the only detention, at Schiphol, ended in release, so escorts protect aircraft without deterring senders. On 10-11 Nov suspected drones from Belarus closed Vilnius and Kaunas airports while NATO jets, scrambled twice, shot nothing down (single source), repeating Romania's failed interception of 31 Oct. Hijacking exposed industrial controls, as in the 2 Nov freezer attacks, still works and remains unattributed. Counter-intelligence is the clearest success: Poland arrested two paid arsonists on 10 Nov, Britain detained a US officer at a NATO corps on suspicion of spying the same day, and Romania said on 11 Nov it stopped an FSB-linked intrusion without data loss. NATO claims Baltic Sentry has superseded cable sabotage (single source).

watches.question: Can Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, the 3rd Army Corps counteroffensive north of Lyman, keep regaining ground and disrupt Russia's planned pincer on the Donbas fortress belt (Lyman–Sviatohirsk in the north, Dobropillia in the south, converging on Barvinkove), how is Russia responding with counterattacks, reserves and narrative, and what does it show about restoring manoeuvre under drone-saturated conditions?

findings.actor: Russian 25th Combined Arms Army and Western Grouping elements

findings.text: A Ukrainian brigade spokesperson said on 10 Nov 2026, relayed by ISW, that Russia is accumulating infantry to cross the Zherebets and regain west-bank positions lost in Vivaldi, but struggles to concentrate because of thinning foliage and Ukrainian fire control over the few remaining crossings. ISW assesses the forest between the Siverskyi Donets and Zherebets east of Yampil may serve as a staging ground; no crossing has succeeded so far.

findings.actor: Russian aviation
findings.tactic: Air strikes on Ukrainian river crossings
findings.text: The Ukrainian spokesperson and a Russian Western Grouping source both said on 10 Nov 2026 that Russia is using aviation to strike Ukrainian crossings over the Oskil and Siverskyi Donets to disrupt logistics behind the Lyman front. No effect on Ukrainian positions has been reported; the same day a Kremlin-affiliated milblogger claimed Ukraine's Lyman offensive has not ended and is trying to shrink the Russian bridgehead.

findings.actor: Russian forces incl. 1st Guards Tank Army elements moved from Kupyansk
findings.tactic: Infantry waves across open fields and river
findings.text: A Ukrainian brigade spokesperson said on 9 Nov 2026 that Russian activity near Lyman had increased, with infantry waves crossing open fields and the Zherebets in a 'suicidal manner' to stabilise the line; ISW, which notes 1st Guards Tank Army elements were shifted from Kupyansk in October, recorded no Russian advance and read the pattern as growing urgency. The waves are a Ukrainian account ISW did not confirm.

findings.actor: Russian forces southeast of Lyman
findings.tactic: Claimed seizure of central Dibrova
findings.text: Russian claims of seizing central Dibrova were disputed on 8 Nov 2026 by a source reporting on Russia's own Western Grouping, who said Ukrainian drones are constraining Russian troops there; the same source reported a Ukrainian counterattack near Balka Zhuravka northeast of Lyman. ISW recorded no Russian advance, so the claim is not borne out.

findings.actor: Russian milbloggers and a Western Grouping source
findings.tactic: Claimed new positions near Maslyakivka
findings.text: Several Russian milbloggers and a Western Grouping source claimed on 7 Nov 2026 that Russian forces were taking new positions near Maslyakivka, just east of Lyman. ISW recorded no advance on 6-7 Nov and Ukrainian counterattacks southeast of Lyman, so the claim is unconfirmed (single source).

findings.actor: 3rd Army Corps (66th Brigade and five other brigades)
findings.tactic: Unified corps command, drone superiority, supply interdiction
findings.text: A New York Times account published on 7 Nov 2026 says Vivaldi worked by seizing high ground to cut Russian communications, shooting down Russian supply drones and blocking roads, gaining an edge in strike and reconnaissance drones that left Russians 'effectively blinded', and placing six brigades under one corps command that sealed the gaps infiltrators had used; the 66th Brigade took one village within a month with infiltration and ambushes. Analysts and Russian milbloggers confirmed the loss of the salient north of Lyman.

findings.actor: 3rd Army Corps logistics units
findings.tactic: Ground robots for front-line resupply
findings.text: The same 7 Nov 2026 New York Times account reports Biletskyi's claim that robotic ground vehicles let his brigades receive three times as much cargo as other recently added brigades, but also that many robots broke down or were destroyed by Russian drones. The logistics gain is the commander's own claim, while the attrition shows the method is still being contested.

findings.actor: 3rd Army Corps unmanned ground systems (per Russian sources)
findings.tactic: Massed 28-robot armed ground assault
findings.text: Russian Telegram channels reported, relayed by Defense Express on 6 Nov 2026, a 3rd Army Corps assault near Lyman by 28 ground robots: two with Mk-19 grenade launchers, 18 with AT-4 launchers and eight kamikaze platforms. Russian sources say they repelled it; there is no Ukrainian statement or footage, so both the scale and the outcome are unconfirmed (single source).

findings.actor: MURAMASA unit, 21st KRAKEN Unmanned Systems Regiment (3rd Army Corps)
findings.tactic: Drone strike on Buk-M3 air defence
findings.text: The 3rd Army Corps reported on 4 Nov 2026 that MURAMASA drone operators detected and struck a Russian Buk-M3 surface-to-air system in the Vivaldi area and released video; Ukrainian outlets valued the system at about US$45m. The strike continues the corps' October hits on Buk-M3 loaders, thinning Russian air defence over its strike drones, but the claim rests on the corps' own footage and does not assert destruction (single source).

findings.actor: Russian Western Grouping of Forces
findings.tactic: Assaults to seize Zarichne northeast of Lyman
findings.text: ISW's 4 Nov 2026 assessment cited a Western Grouping-affiliated source denying Russian claims to control Zarichne, calling it a contested gray zone where Russian units are still struggling to gain a foothold. ISW recorded no confirmed Russian advance in the Lyman direction, and Ukraine's General Staff reported further assaults near Stavky, Dibrova and Zarichne repelled on 5 Nov.

findings.actor: Russian 25th Combined Arms Army and Western Grouping elements
findings.tactic: Attacks east of Lyman, Zarichne and Yampolivka
findings.text: ISW reported that Russian forces concentrated attacks east of Lyman and in the Zarichne and Yampolivka areas on 1-2 Nov 2026 and continued operations within and near Lyman on 2-3 Nov without advancing, while Ukrainian forces counterattacked south, northeast and southeast of Lyman. ISW counts about 7.4 Russian attacks a day in the Lyman direction in October, down from 8.4 in September.

assessment.text: Operation Vivaldi is formally over: the 3rd Army Corps declared on 14 Oct that its 'four seasons' were complete, Biletskyi presented the results and handed the corps to Dmytro Rohoziuk on 19 Oct, and no new phase has been announced since. The fighting it produced continues as a Russian effort to retake the Zherebets line. ISW recorded Russian attacks around Lyman every day from 6 to 11 Nov with no confirmed advance; claims of new positions near Maslyakivka (7 Nov) and central Dibrova (8 Nov) were unconfirmed or disputed by a Russian source citing Ukrainian drones. Russia is adapting with 1st Guards Tank Army reserves, infantry waves across the Zherebets (9 Nov) and air strikes on Oskil and Siverskyi Donets crossings (10 Nov), so far without gains. Unified corps command, drone superiority and supply-drone interdiction worked, per the New York Times on 7 Nov, but many ground robots broke down or were destroyed, and a reported 28-robot assault on 6 Nov rests only on Russian claims that it was repelled.

text: On dense urban operations versus dispersed and concealed networks, the Established and Contested status holds without a ground test: no Hamas attack on troops was reported in the fortnight, and Israel kept shaping the network from the air, saying on 12 Nov that it struck Khan Younis Brigade commander Muhammad Abu Ismail inside Nasser hospital. The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride sank after a projectile hit in the Strait of Hormuz the previous day, one of two ships lost within a day, as security data showed at least ten vessels attacked since 11 October.

The IRGC claimed seven tankers hit overnight in and near the Strait of Hormuz, which Trump called fake and no maritime agency confirmed, a day after the New York Times reported US and Israeli plans for a short, intensive strike campaign on Iran after the 3 November midterms.

On the eve of the US midterms, US forces carried out limited 'defensive' strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island after IRGC surface-to-air fire at US aircraft, which officials said was not a resumption of major combat.
Trump confirmed 'minor' US strikes on Qeshm Island that he said knocked out a small Iranian anti-aircraft system, the first US strikes on Iran since the 3 November midterms.
After meeting Qatar's prime minister, Trump said he would hold off on fresh strikes at Gulf states' request while keeping the naval blockade of Iranian ports in place.
Israel's caretaker security cabinet ordered the military to step up preparations for a possible attack on Iran, as Tehran denied any talks with Washington and kept claiming tanker hits in Hormuz.

text: Long-range strike versus integrated air and missile defence (Established · Contested) is borne out at small scale only: US aircraft hit Qeshm air defences on 2 Nov and again on 6 Nov, which Trump called 'minor', while Iran claimed MQ-1 and MQ-9 kills over the island, so each side is probing the other's air defences without an open campaign. The contest is now a test of whether Israel acts alone, after its cabinet ordered stepped-up preparations on 11 Nov. Maritime chokepoint disruption versus energy-route resilience (Established · Contested) is strongly borne out: Washington has made the port blockade its main lever, with Rubio saying on 10 Nov that major combat is unneeded, while Iran pairs projectile hits reported by operators and UKMTO, as off Oman on 10 and 11 Nov, with unverified mine claims meant to deter use of the US-escorted southern route.

Deterrence versus proxy and deniable escalation (Rising · Contested) is borne out and widening: Iran claimed a strike on Oman's Didamar navigation aids on 10 Nov, which Oman denied, and the same day the US indicted Kataib Hezbollah-linked plotters over RAF Fairford, and on 11 Nov Rezaei threatened bases as far as Europe. Adaptability stays High on all three topics.

timeline.text: The United States, Israel and Lebanon signed a US-brokered Trilateral Framework tying phased Israeli withdrawal to Hezbollah disarmament and creating a trilateral military coordination group.
Israel detonated about 1,100 tonnes of explosives to destroy Hezbollah tunnels under Ali al-Taher ridge and declared its south Lebanon security zone complete.

Hezbollah launched an explosive drone at Israeli troops inside the security zone overnight without causing casualties, the Israeli air force struck drone and anti-tank launch sites across nine southern localities in response, and Qassem told a Nasrallah-anniversary crowd that resistance continues until full expulsion and that Israel must first liberate the south before any dialogue.

Two days of US-hosted Lebanon–Israel military talks at CENTCOM headquarters in Tampa ended without a breakthrough, with Israel rejecting Lebanon's demand for third-party verification of its army's operations.

Lebanon's military prosecutor charged 13 people over the Dahr al-Baidar explosives shipment, including two Hezbollah security officials still at large, and referred the file to an investigating judge.

An Israeli drone strike in Qabrikha, outside the buffer zone, killed a paramedic of the Amal-linked Risala Scouts, the first such fatality in south Lebanon since September, as Lebanon's prime minister warned against joining another war.

Lebanese security forces arrested five Hezbollah members carrying maps and documents on a suspected reconnaissance mission between Batroun and Bsharri, and the prime minister declared an end to impunity.
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem said the group will not give up its weapons, accusing Israel of seeking to disarm Lebanon in order to occupy it.

text: On border-zone security versus rocket, drone and dispersed-launch threats, the Established and Contested status is borne out as a one-sided contest: no Hezbollah fire on troops was reported in the fortnight, while Israel struck outside its zone at Qabrikha on 4 Nov and shelled and struck villages on 9 Nov, and said on 8 Nov it found weapons caches 100–200 m from UNIFIL posts, an Israeli claim that frames the zone as a search-and-clear operation. On precision strike versus escalation control, restraint is holding through politics rather than fire: Qassem on 11 Nov refused to disarm but tied his hopes to Trump's and Netanyahu's election losses, and Washington is reportedly seeking a southern ceasefire to protect its Iran talks (single source).

On ceasefire monitoring versus armed-group reconstitution, the trigger is closer to firing: direct talks were reported suspended on 9 Nov over verification, gunmen fired on a UNIFIL patrol on 10 Nov weeks before its exit, yet the state arrested five Hezbollah members on a suspected reconnaissance mission the same day, so internal enforcement is filling part of the monitoring gap.

timeline.text: Thailand and Cambodia signed a ceasefire taking effect at noon, ending 20 days of fighting that killed over 100 people and displaced more than half a million.
Thailand's armed forces chief announced completion of the first 1.3 km of a permanent concrete border wall in Chanthaburi's Pong Nam Ron district, with over 7 km more planned.

The Hague conciliation round closed with the first agreed confidence-building measures (a direct channel between the two navies among them, by Thailand's account), while the Commission noted earlier measures were unimplemented and set a third meeting in Kuala Lumpur for 24–27 November.

Cambodia's culture ministry demanded the return of artefacts Thailand removed from K'nar temple and called Thai activity at disputed border temples a fait accompli, as the Thai army rejected Cambodian charges that its barbed-wire barriers were redrawing the boundary by force.

Thailand's defence minister said the boundary dispute was unresolved, parked defence-ministry talks in favour of the Regional Border Committee, and said troops facing Cambodian soldiers climbing Hill 642 apply rules of engagement starting with dialogue and warning shots.

China's foreign minister Wang Yi hosted his Cambodian and Thai counterparts for tea in Beijing on the sidelines of the Lancang-Mekong foreign ministers' meeting, discussing confidence-building measures between the two neighbours.

The ASEAN Observer Team visited the Chey Chomneas checkpoint area in Pursat, where Cambodia said Thai forces had moved an observation post about 20 metres forward and kept digging trenches, and the team inspected a bridge destroyed by Thai airstrikes in December 2025.
Thailand's foreign minister said Thailand would attend the Francophonie Summit in Phnom Penh only as an observer and urged Cambodia to keep the border dispute off the summit agenda.

text: On border incident management versus escalation prevention, the Declining / cautiously improving status is borne out more firmly than a week ago: after the late-October warning shots at Hill 642, no exchange of fire, mine casualty or new warning-shot incident was reported from 6 to 12 Nov, and on 9 Nov the Thai army called the eastern border under control while keeping units ready. Restraint still rests on rules of engagement, not a settlement. On ceasefire monitoring versus local force autonomy, the trigger has not fired, but observers are recording consolidation rather than reversing it: on 5 Nov they saw a Thai post moved about 20 metres forward at Chey Chomneas (Cambodian account), and their 12 Nov visit to the closed Kilo 13 crossing produced no published findings. The air force's receipt of KB-5E one-way attack drones on 30 Oct (single source) adds stand-off capacity behind the wire.

On regional mediation versus bilateral military signalling, the Background monitor status holds while the contest moves into forums: on 10 Nov Sihasak said Thailand would attend Cambodia's Francophonie Summit only as an observer and asked Phnom Penh to keep the dispute off its agenda, ahead of the Manila and Kuala Lumpur meetings. Adaptability stays Low.

history.note: Baseline: post-January 2026 operation; transition under US pressure.

timeline.text: US forces captured President Nicolás Maduro and his wife in overnight strikes across Caracas and three other states, flying them to New York to face narco-terrorism charges.
The White House announced 100-year concessions on 17 Venezuelan oil fields to North American Blue Energy Partners, with the US government taking a 35 percent stake.

The third round of government–opposition talks closed with a commitment to review the party, disqualification, sanctions and terrorism laws and to install a Supreme Court nominating committee, with no election date and a fourth round set for 11–15 November.
Opposition leader María Corina Machado returned to Venezuela overland from Colombia after about ten months abroad, greeted by tens of thousands of supporters on the road to Caracas.
Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere struck a go-fast vessel in the Eastern Pacific, killing five, the first announced US lethal boat strike since 4 October.

Venezuelan forces struck an ELN camp in Apure near the Colombian border with helicopters and drones, killing at least 19 people, with US intelligence and drone support according to US officials cited by the New York Times.
The New York Times reported that Washington is negotiating a status-of-forces agreement with Caracas that could underpin a long-term US military presence in Venezuela.
ExxonMobil signed a non-binding memorandum with PDVSA in Caracas to evaluate upstream oil projects, its first step back into Venezuela since 2007.

text: On counter-criminal operations versus sovereignty and escalation, the trigger met on 30 Oct has not deepened: no second strike on Venezuelan soil was confirmed, neither government has claimed the Apure raid, and the “hunter-killer” model described on 11 Nov, with Venezuelan targeting and US drones, remains analyst inference (single source). Consent rather than coercion keeps escalation risk political, not military. On border and maritime control versus illicit networks, the Established status holds but its weight has moved inland and to Colombia: no boat strike was found after 27 Oct, while Bogotá announced a Catatumbo bombing on 9 Nov under Operation Esparta (single source), so spillover pressure now sits on the Colombian side.

On information operations versus political legitimacy, the Rising status is borne out at a slower pace: the opposition said on 8 Nov that only 27 releases were confirmed since late September, the fourth round slipped to 13 Nov without a promised release announcement, and Exxon’s 9 Nov memorandum ties US corporate stakes to Rodríguez before any election date. The partnered-strike model stays the most transferable lesson at Medium adaptability.

Sustained pressure on the Second Thomas Shoal outpost: the resupply run still unscheduled two weeks after the 24 Sep interception, a 10-hour medevac forced through CCG water cannon on 8 Oct, PLA fighters intercepting Philippine patrol aircraft over Scarborough, 101 Chinese ships counted in September, and Manila holding to code-of-conduct diplomacy

Contested resupply and a diplomatic crisis: the Sierra Madre resupplied on 20 Oct for the first time since the 24 Sep interception, with Beijing claiming it 'permitted' the run and Manila denying it; Ambassador Jing summoned on 19 Oct over his 'easily win' remark amid calls for his expulsion, and PLAN ships shadowing USS Charleston at Sabina Shoal on 20 Oct

Surging Chinese naval presence and a deepening diplomatic freeze: 54 Chinese ships at four features on 20-26 Oct (26 PLAN, 7 at Ayungin), the Liaoning group circling the Philippines from 22 Oct, and Beijing downgrading to a defence attaché at the 29 Oct ADMM-Plus in Cebu

Heavy Chinese presence with a thin diplomatic opening: 80 Chinese ships at four features in October (33 PLAN), PLA combat-readiness patrols at Scarborough on 30 Oct and a sensor-laden vessel in its lagoon, then a Lazaro-Wang Yi call on 3 Nov keeping dialogue open before the Manila ASEAN summit, which Xi is expected to skip

items.whyNow: The Manila ASEAN summit (15-18 Nov), with Premier Li Qiang and President Trump attending, is the Philippine chair's last real chance to land a South China Sea code of conduct before Singapore takes over the talks; Manila has toned down its own messaging to help, while China has thinned its presence without conceding anything at Scarborough or Ayungin.
changes: 13 Nov: DFA Undersecretary Leo Herrera-Lim said the code of conduct will probably not be concluded by the summit and needs 'one more meeting', with legal nature, geographic scope, self-restraint and third-party rights still open; ASEAN leaders meet Li Qiang in a special summit during the 15-18 Nov meetings (BusinessMirror).

12 Nov: ASEAN spokesperson Dominic Imperial said '70 percent of the COC package' is agreed but would not say whether it will be concluded before Manila's chairmanship ends in December; Malacañang also declined to confirm a deal at the summit (Philstar; Daily Tribune).

10 Nov: the AFP counted 29 Chinese navy and coast guard ships at four features on 3-8 Nov (10 at Ayungin, 8 at Bajo de Masinloc, 6 at Escoda, 5 at Pag-asa; 9 of them navy), about half the 54 logged in the week to 26 Oct, with no incident reported (GMA News).

8 Nov: the foreign ministry issued a rare rebuke telling civilian and military officials to align with President Marcos's China policy, calling recent statements that 'merged' evidence, rhetoric and diplomacy regrettable and saying 'transparency cannot substitute for statecraft' (GMA News; China-Global South Project).

history.note: Injury, ramming, radar locks and a forward PLAN group at Scarborough; COC deadline at the November summit.

timeline.text: Three PLAN warships, including two Type 022 missile boats, and five China Coast Guard cutters intercepted the MV Lapu-Lapu resupply run about 60 nautical miles from Second Thomas Shoal, a warship radioed that it would take 'compulsory measures' and the mission was suspended, the first blocked run since the July 2024 understanding.

A China Coast Guard cutter trained its water cannon on BRP Cabra during a medical evacuation from BRP Sierra Madre, forcing a small-boat transfer four nautical miles off the reef that delayed the mission by nearly ten hours, while a PLA Navy frigate stood nearby.

The armed forces completed a rotation-and-resupply run to BRP Sierra Madre without incident, the first since the 24 September interception, while China's coast guard said it had approved and monitored the delivery and Manila denied seeking any permission; the same day PLA Navy ships shadowed USS Charleston near Sabina Shoal.

The carrier Liaoning and three destroyers sailed through the Sulu Sea and the Basilan Strait inside the Philippine archipelago, shadowed by Philippine warships, before heading east toward the Philippine Sea, as Chinese navy ships near Philippine-held features rose to 26 in the week to 26 October.

China's Southern Theater Command said its naval and air forces flew combat-readiness patrols around Scarborough Shoal as a countermeasure to Philippine 'provocations', a day after a Philippine patrol flight found an unidentified Chinese vessel with a sensor-fitted craft inside the shoal's lagoon.

The Philippine and Chinese foreign ministers agreed by phone to keep dialogue open and manage differences peacefully, while Beijing's readout accused unnamed Philippine politicians of crossing its red lines.

The Philippine foreign ministry publicly rebuked unnamed officials and agencies for comments on China, saying all must align with the President's policy and that transparency cannot substitute for statecraft.
The ASEAN spokesperson said about 70 percent of the South China Sea code of conduct had been agreed, while a senior diplomat said it would likely not be concluded at the Manila summit.

text: On grey-zone maritime coercion versus presence and resilience, the Established · Contested status holds but is quieter: the AFP counted 29 Chinese ships at four features on 3-8 Nov against 54 in the week to 26 Oct, and no collision, boarding or water-cannon use was reported in the fortnight. Coercion is being held in reserve while Beijing works the summit track, where Manila said on 12 Nov that 70% of the code is agreed but its legal nature and scope remain open. On maritime domain awareness versus ambiguous attribution, the Rising status is contradicted at the political level: the 3 Nov disclosure of an unidentified sensor-carrying vessel in the Scarborough lagoon was followed on 8 Nov by a foreign ministry rebuke saying transparency 'cannot substitute for statecraft', which narrows Manila's most effective adaptation of the past two years.

On distributed maritime posture versus force protection, the Rising · Contested rating is supported: even at lower totals, Chinese hulls were spread across Ayungin (10), Scarborough (8), Escoda (6) and Pag-asa (5) on 3-8 Nov, so each dispersed Philippine outpost still faces a standing picket and adaptability remains Medium.

changes: 12 Nov: Xi called resolving the Taiwan question an 'unwavering historical mission' and said reunification 'will certainly be realised', which the Mainland Affairs Council rejected; Taiwan detected 29 PLA aircraft, including J-16s and drones, on a joint combat readiness patrol with warships (single source for the patrol) (Al Jazeera).

11 Nov: G7 foreign ministers said China's activity east of Taiwan threatens regional stability, freedom of navigation and the safety of shipping, their strongest joint statement to date; the Presidential Office welcomed it (Reuters via Taipei Times).

timeline.text: The military launches 'Operation 4926', a combined land, naval and air offensive against the Arakan Army across Sittwe, Ponnagyun, Kyaukphyu and Gwa townships in Rakhine State.

Junta warships, artillery and aircraft begin a week of failed landing attempts on Ngapyi Island opposite the Shwe Min Gan naval base near Sittwe, and by 14 October the Arakan Army still holds the island and has taken outposts on the city's edge, by local accounts.

The Arakan Army reportedly struck three navy vessels, including a frigate, near the Kaladan river mouth by the Shwe Min Gan naval base off Sittwe, sinking two, by anonymous military and AA-side accounts.

Junta airstrikes on four Rakhine townships killed at least 12 people, including a newborn at a makeshift maternity clinic in Arakan Army-held Mrauk-U, a day after a strike on a school in Loikaw killed three students.

Regime forces retook Alel, one of three villages on Ngapyi Island opposite the Shwe Min Gan naval base, by an anonymous Arakan Army source, after a counteroffensive reinforced with 1,000 troops on 30 October.

Three regime gyrocopters bombed a school and homes in Nyaung Pin Lay village in Sagaing, killing 11 people including four children, after a resistance warning could not reach the village because it had no internet.

text: On distributed resistance versus state airpower, the Established · Contested status holds but tilted toward the regime this fortnight: state media claimed on 10 Nov that a six-day operation on the Mon–Bago border took the NUG's special region command and a KNLA battalion headquarters, unrebutted but unconfirmed, while near Sittwe the regime regained only Alel village on 4 Nov (single source) and no change was reported for 6–12 Nov. Ground gains are coming where resistance forces are thinnest, not where the Arakan Army is strongest. On commercial UAS and improvised systems versus conventional advantage, the Rising status is not contradicted but cuts both ways: the regime flew three low gyrocopters to kill 11 people, four of them children, at Nyaung Pin Lay in Sagaing on 7 Nov (single source), and the seized Mon–Bago bases reportedly held resistance drone units.

On fragmented governance versus logistics and civilian resilience, the Established status is reinforced: the Kani strike killed because a resistance warning could not reach a village without internet, with Starlink terminals disabled and phone lines cut in over 40 per cent of townships (RFA, 10 Nov), while Thailand stepped up Mae Sot patrols on 8 Nov and its foreign minister visited Myanmar on 12 Nov. Adaptability stays High.
